What is an online fringe group in simple words?This would be friends only on line and even then they are not close friends as they are not on the list of your favourite people!!!!Can a small group of people affect society change if they are loud enough?According the United States Supreme Court, in the Citizens United case, money = free speech. Thus, if you have a small group of people with a great deal of money, their free speech ability will be correspondingly great, probably enough to drown out the other, less-wealthy voices. In order for a cash-poor small group to affect societal change, it is not enough that they be simply loud: there’s so much noise in the political conversation these days that people can tune out those who only have volume on their side. Those wishing to generate change will have to add persuasion to their voice - through through appeals to fear, logic, shared values, patriotism, etc. A loud voice with a bad message (“Steam video games should be free every Friday!”) will be ignored, while a strong voice with a good message (“Too many children are struck down by Congenital Heart Disease, and we need to invest more in research”) might be able to attract other people to the cause, changing the group from small to large.Can a small group of people affect society change if they are loud enough?Sometimes it’s not Loud but noble, fervent, peaceful but willing to die for what they belief.Sponsored by BetweenUs.caWhen Was the Last Time You Really Talked?Not about groceries or schedules — actually talked. BetweenUs is a free conversation tool.How can groups resist being unduly influenced by outsiders or powerful members?It is difficult. Often the group’s charter proves its downfall — forcing it to accept members from organizations that (on occasion) are people intent on working at cross-purposes to the group’s intended function. I once sat on a board that organized the Colorado Science Fair. One of its express goals was to enlist interest and participation from large companies with a perceived focus on science and engineering concerns, and yet rein them in from taking the affair over and turning it into just a promotion gimmick for their brand. You can guess what happened. One of the industry participants was a guy with boundless ego, a complete disregard for the bylaws, a loud booming voice, and enough testosterone to fuel a battleship. He quickly overrode the parliamentary procedure that underlays every well-structured meeting, evicted both the Secretary and parliamentarian, bulled his way to the top of the heap and proceeded to use the meager funds on hand for outreach to schools to attract student involvement and instead instituted an ad-campaign. For his organization. That was the point where my gut told me to bail. Mind you, this wasn’t a limp artifact from a bygone era that was held together by rusty staples and a dab of mucilage — the board had functioned smoothly since the early 1960’s, and had close ties to IEEE, ACM, and maybe another dozen or so professional organizations of the top-caliber. I gather from later evidence that they tossed the guy out, reconstructed the charter to expressly forbid corporate figures from board participation, and scrabbled enough resources together to carry off that year’s event (albeit in a fairly meek imitation of its usual grandeur), and carry on with an 11th-hour save. I wished I’d stayed long enough to see the blowhard physically manhandled out of the boardroom after being yanked off the membership and a rather fierce letter sent to the CEO of his company explaining why his “guy” was no longer welcome. Enough said. Similar problems can arise when your organization is beholden to an external partner who in turn is influenced by dark forces. My advice?
